evidence.text: Simplified form of 漢; the Han 𦰩 river 氵
Phonosemantic compound. 氵 represents the meaning and 堇 represents the sound.  The simplified character 汉 was adapted from the cursive form of the traditional character 漢.
Simplified from 漢 (elimination of right component to 又 (yòu)) in the 1956 Chinese Character Simplification Scheme by the People's Republic of China. Not known to have existed prior to that.

The Han 𦰩 river 氵
Phonosemantic compound. 氵 represents the meaning and 堇 represents the sound.
漾也。東爲滄浪水。从水，難省聲。

Earliest attested in early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions; the 京師畯尊 preserves the form ⿰氵⿱𦰩火. Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hnaːns): semantic 水 (“water”) + phonetic 𦰩 — name of the Han River. 𦰩 (phonetic; a bound person crying out, probable original form of 嘆 /叹 (tàn)) became confused with 黃 /黄 (huáng) as early as the 伯△鼎 (銘續 0213), and by the Spring and Autumn period the corruption was nearly complete. ⿱𦰩火 (transcribable as 堇 (qín) or 熯) may relate to the oracle bone sacrificial practice of burning disabled people (尪 (wāng)) to pray for rain (⿱黃火).
The usage for the Chinese ethnicity first appeared during the Northern and Southern Dynasties, claiming the Han dynasty as one of the golden ages of Chinese history. Before the Han dynasty, the Chinese referred their land as 華夏 ("Huaxia"), and themselves as 諸華 ("various Hua people") or 諸夏 ("various people/descendants of the Xias"). "Xia" ("Summer; great, splendid") also gave the name to the first semi-legendary Chinese dynasty, the Xia Dinasty (夏朝).

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 漢 entry (historical forms and analysis; secondary compilation)
evidence.field: glyph origin; earliest attestation; semantic and phonetic components
evidence.text: The entry identifies an early Western Zhou bronze inscription, 京師畯尊, with the phrase 王涉漢伐楚, where 漢 names a river. It analyzes the graph as 水 plus a phonetic element transcribed 熯, and reports that the upper component 𦰩 may have become confused with 黃 from the middle Western Zhou onward. This supports an early river-name use and a water semantic element, but the phonetic analysis and graphic sequence are claims of this compilation, not direct visual verification here.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 吳鎮烽, Fudan University Center for Research on Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.text: The author reports examining the 京師畯尊 and gives the inscription phrase 王涉漢伐楚. He correlates it with the received Bamboo Annals account of King Zhao crossing the Han to campaign against Chu, dating the vessel to that campaign. This supports the inscription reading as a river reference; its proposed historical dating is an epigraphist’s argument, not an independently established absolute date in the page.
evidence.title: 吳鎮烽：京師畯尊釋文補正

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: Shuowen account; traditional graph and senses
evidence.text: The entry records the received Shuowen explanation: 漢 is a river, glossed 漾, flowing east as 滄浪水, and is written 从水、難省聲. It also preserves Xu Xuan’s note that 難省聲 should perhaps be 堇, while noting transmission of the received wording. The entry lists river, Milky Way, dynasty, ethnic/cultural, and later personal senses with classical citations. These are dictionary attestations and quotations, not a proven chronological chain between senses.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 漢 entry (phonology section citing Baxter–Sagart and Zhengzhang systems)
evidence.text: Modern Standard Mandarin is hàn (Pinyin), Cantonese is hon3 (Jyutping). The entry gives Middle Chinese xanH and Old Chinese *n̥ˤar-s in Baxter–Sagart (2014), with a Western dialect development note, and *hnaːns in Zhengzhang (2003). The reconstructions are system-specific; they make a historical sound relationship worth investigating but do not themselves prove which ancient graph supplied the sound.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction, version 1.1 data table
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction; scope and notation
evidence.text: The authors identify their table as Old Chinese reconstructions in the Baxter–Sagart system and distinguish reconstructed Old Chinese from Middle Chinese transcriptions. Search-indexed table content lists 漢 hàn, MC xanH, OC *n̥ˤar-s, with the gloss river name and a proposed Western dialect development. The directly opened PDF was inspected for its explanatory conventions, but its searchable page text did not expose the 漢 row; the row-specific wording was visible in the search result only and is therefore not treated as independently inspected page text.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.text: The entry gives modern Mandarin 堇 qín and Middle Chinese gin for one reading, with Old Chinese reconstructions varying by system and reading: Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]rə[r] and Zhengzhang *ɡrɯn. These are useful comparisons for the proposed 堇 analysis, but they do not closely match 漢’s cited *n̥ˤar-s / *hnaːns without additional historical explanation. The entry also gives an alternative visual interpretation of an ancient 堇 graph as a person in a rain sacrifice; it should not be treated as settled origin evidence for 漢’s sound component.
evidence.title: 堇 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Mark C. Elliott, Hushuo: The Northern Other and the Naming of the Han Chinese
evidence.text: The abstract dates the beginning of the process by which Han came to name the Central Plains people as early as the sixth century CE and argues the meaning stabilized only much later, after the Ming began. This cautions against treating Han as a timeless ethnic label. The abstract does not supply the earliest dated textual example.
evidence.title: Hushuo: The Northern Other and the Naming of the Han Chinese

evidence.source: The Multifaceted Saga of the Ethnonym Han, Sino-Platonic Papers 371
evidence.field: river-to-fief-to-dynasty naming sequence; early dynastic sense
evidence.text: The study explains the Han fief and dynasty name through the Han River and Hanzhong, citing Shiji and the Eastern Jin Huayang guozhi account that Hanzhong was named for the river. It distinguishes the Han dynasty’s political label and Hanren, and discusses scholarly disagreement over when Han became an ethnic self-designation. This supports the naming sequence but not an exact first date for every use.
evidence.title: The Multifaceted Saga of the Ethnonym Han

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: modern traditional-form readings and separate senses
evidence.text: The dictionary records Mandarin hàn and quotes the Book of Odes for both the Han River (江漢) and the Milky Way (天漢). It also gives later senses for dynasty, Han people and Chinese cultural terms, with citations including Northern Wei, Tang, and later texts. Since the entry groups senses rather than establishing a semantic chronology, these citations should be used individually, not read as a simple extension sequence.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: People's Republic of China Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The official resolution is dated 1956-01-28 and states that the first table of 230 simplified characters was to become standard in printed and written documents nationwide from 1956-02-01. The opened page attempt returned an internal error; this was found in the actual search result text, so the resolution’s broad date is recorded while 汉’s individual table position remains unverified from the page.
evidence.title: 国务院关于公布汉字简化方案的决议(1956年)

evidence.text: The entry describes 汉 as the simplified form corresponding to 漢, with the right-side component 𦰩 replaced by 又 in simplified Chinese. This is a modern graphic relationship; it does not establish that the traditional right-side graph historically meant 又 or that the whole graph was borrowed for another word.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Taiwan Ministry of Education variant dictionary, as accessed page
evidence.field: received small-seal analysis and shape note
evidence.text: The entry says the received Shuowen seal form has 水 plus an abbreviated 難 phonetic, and its standard printed right portion is written in a shape also indexed as a variant of 堇. It explicitly preserves uncertainty in Xu Xuan’s note about how the sound element should be named. This supports documenting competing analyses rather than confidently assigning 堇 as the original ancestor.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 吳鎮烽, Shaanxi Provincial Institute of Archaeology, hosted by Fudan University Center for Research on Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.text: The author says he examined and photographed the 京師畯尊 and reads 王涉漢伐楚, interpreting it as the king crossing the Han River to attack Chu. He argues for a date during King Zhao’s campaign by comparing the inscription with the received Bamboo Annals. This is an epigraphist’s reading and dating argument, not an absolute date established on the page.
evidence.title: 吳鎮烽：京師畯尊釋文補正

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: received Shuowen account and component analysis
evidence.text: The entry reports the received Shuowen gloss 漾也。東為滄浪水 and analysis 从水，難省聲. It preserves Xu Xuan’s note that 難省聲 should perhaps be 堇, while observing that the transmitted writing has continued. Its shape note says the regular-script right part is also indexed as a variant of 堇. This records competing textual analyses; it does not establish the right component’s original ancestor.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: early graph analysis and reported graphic change
evidence.text: The entry associates 漢 in the 京師畯尊 with a Western Zhou river-name attestation and analyzes it as water plus 熯, reconstructed there as Old Chinese *n̥ˤanʔ. It reports that the upper graphic element 𦰩 may have become confused with 黃 from the middle Western Zhou onward. These are secondary paleographic assertions, not direct visual verification here.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.field: Han character pronunciation and reconstruction comparison
evidence.text: The entry gives modern Beijing Mandarin hàn (Pinyin), Middle Chinese xanH in Baxter’s notation, and Old Chinese *n̥ˤar-s in the Baxter–Sagart system, with a stated Western dialect development. It gives Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese *hnaːns separately. The entries belong to different reconstruction systems; they do not alone prove which ancient graph supplied the sound.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 漢 entry (Zhengzhang phonetic series table)
evidence.text: The entry places 漢 in a Zhengzhang (2003) series under 暵, gives 漢 *hnaːns, and lists related forms including 熯 *hnaːnʔ, *hnaːns and 難 *n̥ʰaːn, *naːns. This supplies a historical sound comparison within the named system, but does not settle whether the early inscription’s right part should be normalized as 熯, 難, 堇, or another form.
evidence.title: 漢 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Book of Odes for the river (江漢) and Milky Way (天漢) senses, and gives later dictionary or literary citations for dynasty, Han people, Chinese cultural terms, and person senses. These individual quotations document uses, but the grouped list is not a semantic chronology. The entry gives Mandarin hàn (Bopomofo ㄏㄢˋ).
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: earliest accessible dictionary evidence for river and Milky Way uses
evidence.text: The dictionary attributes both a Han River quotation (滔滔江漢) and a Milky Way quotation (維天有漢) to the Book of Odes, and cites the received Shuowen for the river gloss. These are dictionary-reported textual examples; the page does not give manuscript dates or prove when the two senses first arose.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry associates later usage as an ethnic-cultural label with Han dynasty prestige, lists 汉语/漢語, 漢字 and 漢學 as cultural terms, and gives Northern Wei, Tang and later quotations for some person senses. It does not establish a first securely dated ethnonym use or a single continuous semantic chain.
evidence.title: A02308 漢 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The entry records 𦰩 as a variant graph with a shape also analyzed as 艹 over a combined 口 and 夫 form, and links it to 漢 among other derived characters. Its data also treats that visual form as a variant of 堇 in another analysis. This illustrates why visual resemblance and later variant listings cannot by themselves determine the early sound component’s name or origin.
evidence.title: 𦰩 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No image of the 京師畯尊 inscription was visually inspected in this research pass. The Fudan article reports the inscription phrase 王涉漢伐楚 and discusses dating, but the identification and absolute dating ultimately depend on epigraphic scholarship.

The source literature consulted does not establish the original spoken name of the Han River, nor whether it was inherited, borrowed, or formed within early Chinese. No whole-graph phonetic loan is demonstrated; the graph is reported as a water-semantic compound used for a river name.

The identification of the 漢 right-side element varies: received Shuowen says 難省聲; Xu Xuan’s note suggests 堇; later paleographic compilations relate the shape to 𦰩/熯 and possible confusion with 黃. The original referent of 𦰩 and the precise graphic transitions remain uncertain. No depicted weapon/tool borrowing claim was found or relied upon.

The cited 堇 pronunciations and 漢 reconstructions do not by themselves establish a direct phonetic match. The separate phonetic history of 𦰩/熯 in the exact early inscriptional form requires specialist paleographic and phonological verification; the early graph’s right element is not confidently normalized here.

The ethnonym chronology is contested and the sources consulted provide broad periodization rather than the earliest securely dated textual occurrence of 漢人 as ethnicity, distinguished from political subjects of the Han dynasty. The language sense and later male/person senses also need independently dated attestations before linking them semantically.

The Shuowen is a Han-period received account, not direct evidence of the Western Zhou graph’s original construction. The MOE entry’s component description reflects standard textual tradition and preserves an explicit ancient uncertainty.

The 1956 official resolution page could not be opened. Search-result text verifies the general scheme effective date, but this research did not verify the exact table listing or any claim that 汉 had no earlier cursive or popular antecedent.

The web search surfaced Xiaoxuetang glyph records whose displayed labels were unrelated characters. They were excluded; no verified Xiaoxuetang 漢 glyph record or exact query-interface image was obtained in this pass.

The Fudan article reports the 京師畯尊 reading 王涉漢伐楚 and argues for a King Zhao campaign date, but a reader comment on the same page disputes part of the inscription’s interpretation. The phrase and date should remain attributed to named scholarly readings rather than treated as uncontested absolute dating.

The right-side component’s earliest referent and original pronunciation are not securely established by the inspected sources. The received Shuowen analysis, Xu Xuan’s correction, and secondary paleographic normalization differ. No whole-graph phonetic borrowing is demonstrated; no depicted weapon/tool name is needed or established.

The *n̥ˤar-s and *hnaːns reconstructions are for 漢 in their respective systems. The inspected sources do not independently establish an ancient pronunciation for a depicted referent or prove that a normalized 堇 reading was the phonetic in the earliest form.

The attested Western Zhou inscription gives an early river-name use, but the sources inspected do not establish the Han River name’s prehistory or whether its name was inherited, borrowed, or coined in early Chinese.

The Book of Odes citations establish dictionary-reported river and Milky Way examples but not their first dates or semantic direction. Exact dated earliest attestations of ethnonym, language, and person senses remain unresolved; a list of later dictionary senses cannot supply the missing chronology.
No actual query image from a Xiaoxuetang record relevant to 漢 was selected. The two proposed visual candidates are modern redrawings; neither has been visually inspected in this research pass.

The direct image for the Warring States redraw could not be fetched because the web viewer returned a cache-miss error. The composite file endpoint was reached but the viewer did not render SVG content. The source descriptions support retaining both as documented candidates, but their pixels were not visually inspected in this pass.
